sourceBindings.text: Record the field's texture, structure, drainage, pH, nutrient test, irrigation or rainfall, temperature and season before narrowing candidates. Sandy soil often drains readily but may retain less water and soluble nutrients. Clay-rich soil can retain more cations and water yet may be difficult to work if compacted or wet. Loam balances particle fractions, but the word alone does not certify drainage, aeration or fertility. Keep local terms for sand, loam and clay distinct when translating them.

Match each crop's actual requirements with measured or observed site qualities. A group-level association is only a first clue. A carrot root needs a workable, unobstructed rooting zone, not one compulsory texture label. Some cereals tolerate wet conditions better than others; do not call all grains flood-tolerant. Soil structure, slope, water table and salinity may overturn a simple texture guess.

sourceBindings.text: Soil pH measures acidity or alkalinity. The classroom range pH 6.0–7.0 is a useful example for many crops, but 6.0 is slightly acidic, 7.0 is neutral and no single range suits every crop. Blueberry is a deliberate exception: it requires a distinctly acidic, well-drained root zone; pH 6.2 should not be treated as a ready blueberry site. The crop variety, soil test and local guidance determine whether adjustment is feasible.

Read nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium results as separate test findings rather than substituting soil colour or texture. A low-N report does not prove that nitrogen alone caused a yield decline, and adequate P/K in a teaching case is not permission to skip all later testing or management.

sourceBindings.text: Lettuce and wheat illustrate cooler-season options; maize and tomato illustrate warmer-season options. This is a seasonal comparison, not a universal planting calendar. Match the crop and variety to the local temperature range and growing-season length. Compare crop water needs with reliable rainfall and irrigation; sorghum can be a relatively drought-tolerant candidate, but drought tolerance does not mean no water is needed.

Light intensity, direct sunlight and day length affect growth, flowering or maturity differently among crops. Six to eight hours of direct sun is a common full-sun example, not a shared requirement of every crop. State actual site light and crop requirements before ruling a crop in or out. For an Egyptian location, gather its verified climate, season and water data; a renamed temperate case remains a temperate case.

sourceBindings.text: A sticky field where water stands for days might contain much clay, but the observation alone does not prove the texture class. Compaction, a restrictive horizon, a high water table or a blocked outlet can also keep water at the surface. Examine the profile, drainage and texture before choosing an action.

Carrot is a reasonable crop to question in a persistently wet or physically obstructed rooting zone because its enlarged root may deform or suffer poor aeration. Do not prescribe a different crop or a drainage treatment until the actual cause and crop requirements are checked.

sourceBindings.text: The classroom farmer has a 10-hectare field with sandy loam, pH 6.2 (slightly acidic), low tested nitrogen and adequate tested phosphorus and potassium. Its stated climate is temperate with moderate rainfall, suitable in the exercise for warm- and cool-season candidates. Maize has been grown for three successive years and the reported yield has declined. The location is unfilled, so these climate statements cannot be presented as observations from an Egyptian site.

The activity has four linked parts: 10 minutes analysing candidates, 10 minutes choosing a year-one response, 15 minutes building and explaining a three-year sequence, and 10 minutes comparing plans with a group (45 minutes total). This step completes the site analysis and immediate recommendation; the next rotation step retains and assesses the full three-year plan and comparison. Group talk supports learning, while each student must submit their own reasoning.

Mr Evans · 10-hectare temperate teaching case. Supplied classroom facts, not your field measurements. The location is unspecified. Keep climate, soil and crop history unchanged; no Egyptian locality is verified. Groups of 3–4 use pens/paper or this worksheet. The four parts total 45 active minutes: 10 analysis + 10 first-year choice here; 15 three-year plan + 10 comparison in the next step. The separate 2-minute setup is preparation, not silently included in 45. Every learner submits their own reasoning. A fourth year, clover cover crop, market/equipment discussion, crop glossary and drawn plan remain extensions.

sourceBindings.text: Write at least two candidates per group and explain each. The worked case proposes maize and barley (grains); soybean and clover or alfalfa (legumes); carrot or potato plus lettuce or spinach (vegetables); strawberry and melon (fruits). Retain these alternatives as possibilities, not proven fits. Check variety and season, soil test, drainage, water, pests, available equipment and market before advising planting. Soybean and forage/cover legumes may have different harvest and land-use purposes.

Strawberry is not an orchard tree, and a clover or alfalfa stand, a perennial fruit planting or another continuing crop may occupy land beyond a one-year annual slot. Ask how long it establishes and remains, whether it is harvested or terminated, and what its pH and drainage requirements are. Do not force a perennial into a one-season rotation table without stating those consequences.

sourceBindings.text: Because tested nitrogen is low after three maize crops, a suitable legume is a reasonable group to investigate for year one, subject to crop fit, compatible nodulation, season, water, pest history and the intended harvest or cover-crop use. Its nitrogen fixation and later credit are conditional and measurable, not a guaranteed replacement for all fertiliser. Declining yield might also reflect water, compaction, pests, disease, salinity or other constraints; collect evidence before deciding why it fell.

An extension challenge may ask for a fourth year, a clover cover crop, market/equipment implications or a crop glossary and diagram. These enrich the adviser exercise; they do not override the crop requirements or the time a perennial remains in the field. The three-year sequence and year-by-year justifications are taught and assessed in the following step.
